western.temperament: Compassionate, empathic, intuitive and adaptable; creative. Shadow: easily wounded, can turn codependent, absorbs other people's moods, drifts into escapism and avoidance. The two fish swim in opposite directions, the classic image of Piscean duality.

chinese.temperament: Brave, competitive, confident, charming, a natural leader; can be impetuous, irritable, stubborn, poor at preparing ahead, and slow to trust and open up.
chinese.clash: Monkey (Wikipedia also lists Snake as the harm pair)

symbolism.meaning: The species has Maori names: popoiangore in Te Aka Maori Dictionary, and pakaka in Te Ara. Te Ara notes vagrants haul out on New Zealand beaches, especially Otago. No traditional story about the animal was found; use the names only.

A female leopard seal living in Waitemata Harbour was named He owha na oku tupuna, 'treasured gift from our ancestors', shortened to Owha. DOC calls her the longest tracked leopard seal in the world; sightings she inspired helped DOC reclassify leopard seals as resident in New Zealand in 2019. A modern naming, not old lore, but a real one with a named hapu.

A leopard seal chased Thomas Orde-Lees over the ice, dropped into the water, tracked his shadow under the ice and surfaced in front of him; Frank Wild shot it. The hunter that reads you from below the surface.

symbolism.culture: Modern natural history (Paul Nicklen, National Geographic)
symbolism.meaning: Over four days one female leopard seal brought photographer Paul Nicklen live, then dead, penguins. The article reads it as an attempt to feed a 'useless predator'. One encounter, one seal, a journalist's reading.

Male leopard seals call for hours in the breeding season, sometimes 13 hours straight, building individual songs from five sounds; the songs are about as predictable as human nursery rhymes. A predator that sings lullaby-simple songs alone under the ice.

The Chinese name is 豹海豹 bào hǎi bào, literally 'leopard sea-leopard' (海豹 hǎi bào is the word for seal). The Tiger idiom 臥虎藏龍 wò hǔ cáng lóng, 'crouching tiger, hidden dragon', means hidden talent and people who are not what they seem.

Generic 'leopard seal spirit animal' meanings (fearlessness, adaptability) appear only on totem blogs. No Indigenous Antarctic tradition exists; the continent had no human population. Do not invent one.

fusion.temperament: Our reading: yang Wood (Tiger) in mutable Water (Pisces). The Tiger wants the apex; Pisces wants to drift and feel the current. The Leopard Seal is the apex animal that drifts: solitary in the pack ice, a wanderer that turns up on beaches far north, then holds the top of the food web without fuss once it is in the water. The Piscean sea gives the Tiger somewhere to range rather than fight.
fusion.gifts: Our reading: range (a grip and a sieve in one mouth), patience under the surface, a generous streak that shows up as provision, a voice that repeats until someone learns the pattern.
fusion.shadow: Our reading: Pisces escapism plus Tiger mistrust. Disappears under the ice when hurt, then surfaces abruptly. Feeds people what it thinks they need rather than asking. Lumbering and defensive on any ground that is not its own.
fusion.love: Our reading: slow to approach, then intensely attentive; love expressed as bringing things. Needs a partner who will stay in the water with it rather than ask it to live on the floe. Pisces tenderness under Tiger pride, so rejection is taken hard and quietly.
fusion.money: Our reading: an opportunist feeder in the AAD's sense ('eat almost anything'): many small income streams plus the occasional big catch. Risk is Tiger impulsiveness meeting Pisces avoidance: big moves, then not opening the statements.
fusion.conflict: Our reading: avoids open fights, watches, then acts once and decisively. Can carry a grievance a long way, like a seal tracking a shadow. Practice: surface earlier and say it on the ice, before it becomes a lunge.

candidate_lines: Under the pack ice you can hold still a long time, reading a shadow on the surface before deciding whether it is worth rising for.
On the floe you look slow, almost clumsy, and you have made your peace with that; the water is where you keep your real speed.
Some winters you sing the same five notes for hours under the ice, the same order day after day, and the one who learns your pattern has learned you.
Once you decide someone is yours to look after, you keep bringing them penguins long after it is clear they will never catch one themselves.
Your mouth carries a grip for the big prey and a sieve for the krill, and you can change from one to the other in the middle of a dive.
A Tiger under the fish sign can drift a very long way north, haul out in a harbor nobody planned for, and treat the pontoon as if it had been waiting.

fact_audit.fact: Header hanzi 豹 (rail__han and serial-han), shown with pinyin bào
fact_audit.note: 豹 bào means leopard, the big cat. The animal's Chinese name is 豹海豹 bào hǎi bào (same in traditional characters); Chinese Wikipedia also lists 豹形海豹 bào xíng hǎi bào and 豹斑海豹 bào bān hǎi bào. If one glyph is needed, 海豹 hǎi bào (seal) is closer than 豹.

fact_audit.fact: Second largest seal in the Antarctic
Hydrurga leptonyx is named for its spotted coat and wide gape, traits shared with the big cat
fact_audit.note: The scientific name does not refer to spots or gape: leptonyx is 'thin-clawed' and Hydrurga is glossed 'water worker' (Wikipedia flags that gloss for verification). Only the English common name 'leopard' points to the spotted coat. The gape clause is unverifiable.

fact_audit.fact: Postcanine teeth have three interlocking cusps, letting it filter krill like baleen whales while still biting large prey
fact_audit.note: Hocking et al. 2013 describe tricuspid postcanines that interlock and form a sieve; seals suck prey in and expel water through the tooth row. Captive trials used fish, and wild krill filtering is inferred (e.g. over 10,000 krill in one stomach), so 'filters krill' should be phrased as 'is equipped to'.

fact_audit.fact: Individual leopard seals have repeatedly approached scuba divers to offer penguins, which researchers describe as provisioning a perceived inferior predator
fact_audit.note: The documented case is one female seal and one photographer, Paul Nicklen, over four days, bringing live then dead penguins. The 'useless predator' interpretation is the article's, not a research finding. Rewrite as Nicklen's encounter.

fact_audit.fact: Females are significantly larger than males, averaging 3 metres and 260 kg, an unusual reversal of the pinniped pattern
fact_audit.note: AAD: females average 3.0 m and 370 kg, males 2.8 m and 320 kg, 'slightly smaller'; large females exceed 3.5 m and 500 kg. So 260 kg is wrong and 'significantly' overstates it. 'Unusual reversal' not checked against a source: UNVERIFIABLE, cut it.

fact_audit.fact: Underwater vocalizations among the most acoustically complex of any pinniped, with harmonic sequences lasting several hours
fact_audit.note: Males do call for hours, sometimes 13 hours straight, in the breeding season. But Chambers, Buck and Rogers 2025 found the songs use five call types and are about as predictable as nursery rhymes, the opposite of 'most complex'. The page's own citation (Rogers and Bryden 1995) was not opened.

fact_audit.fact: Preys on krill, fish, squid, penguins and other seals; one of the widest diets of any Antarctic apex predator
fact_audit.note: AAD: 'eat almost anything', including penguins, fish, squid, crustaceans and the pups of crabeater, Weddell and fur seals. The 'widest of any' ranking is unverifiable; say 'eats almost anything'.

fact_audit.fact: On land it moves in an awkward undulating crawl; rear flippers cannot rotate beneath the body
fact_audit.note: True of all true seals (Phocidae), not special to this species: hind flippers are bound to the pelvis and cannot rotate forward, so they 'galumph'. Wikipedia notes leopard seals have unusually large front flippers.

fact_audit.fact: Proverb of the year: 猛虎藏爪 měng hǔ cáng zhǎo, 'the fierce tiger hides its claws; still water runs deep'
fact_audit.note: Not found as an attested chengyu; the second half is an English proverb glued on. The page labels the pairing as its own, but presents the phrase as a proverb. Real alternative: 臥虎藏龍 wò hǔ cáng lóng, hidden talent.
